591	## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening
592	
593	**Principle.** CI is the default production writer, so it is the main target. Short-lived,
594	least-privilege credentials per job. Every CI dependency is pinned. Agent-written code passes the same
595	checks as human code (S10).
596	
597	**On Papaya's stack**
598	
599	- **Credentials:** OIDC instead of keys and tokens in repository secrets, which any writer can read
600	  (📖 R3.4.1, R3.5.3b). Org default for `GITHUB_TOKEN` set to "restricted", `permissions:` per job (📖 R3.5.3).
601	  "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" off (📖 R3.3.3). Serverless License Key in
602	  SSM, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8). Until G1/G2 are solved, k0s and Firebase
603	  deploys may need a stored credential in GitHub: a kubeconfig or token for k0s, a Firebase token or
604	  service-account key for Firebase Hosting. The owner accepts this as an exception to S2 = 0 until it
605	  is checked whether k0s and Firebase deploys can use OIDC (OD1, OD6). Conditions [design]:
606	  - stored only as an **environment secret** of a protected environment (`production-k0s`, below), never as a repository secret. Anyone
607	    with write access can read repository secrets (📖 R3.5.3b), which would turn the exception into
608	    standing prod write for every engineer and their agent. Environment secrets and a deployment
609	    branch rule limited to `main` are available on Team for private repos (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3), and
610	    only the reviewed deploy workflow references the environment (layer 3);
611	  - the deploy job runs on GitHub-hosted runners. On self-hosted runners, jobs "are not run in an
612	    isolated container, even if they use environments", so environment secrets there must be
613	    treated like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5). Self-hosted runners "can be persistently
614	    compromised by untrusted code" from anyone who can open a PR, and runner groups limit only which
615	    repositories use them (📖 R3.5.2); in a monorepo any workflow can likely target the runner's label (⚠️ G15).
616	    How to restrict a runner to one workflow is not researched (⚠️ G15); just-in-time runners exist
617	    (📖 R3.5.2, not read in detail). If reaching k0s needs a self-hosted runner, that
618	    runner is dedicated to the `production` deploy, and the residual risk is recorded;
619	  - that environment secret is the single source of truth: no copy elsewhere (OD1);
620	  - an owner, an expiry and rotation in the exception register;
621	  - a separate environment `production-k0s` (required since OD24, was optional), limited to
622	    `main` and referenced only by the k0s/Firebase deploy workflow, so AWS deploy jobs cannot read
623	    these secrets [design];
624	  - for k0s, the credential is the namespaced, time-limited ServiceAccount token of layer 1
625	    (OD24), rotated before it expires, and the cluster writes a Kubernetes API audit log: k0s has
626	    none by default and enables it only through `spec.api.extraArgs`, "outside k0s support"
627	    (📖 R9.3.1, R9.3.2). Secrets and token requests are logged at `Metadata` level so their
628	    contents stay out of the log (📖 R9.3.3; examples E11). A leaked token is then limited to
629	    deploys in its namespaces and leaves a trace; shipping that log to the log archive is part
630	    of G1.
631	
632	  Residual risk: admins can change the environment, and a deleted environment comes back without
633	  protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); the alerts and settings comparison in layer 7 cover this. The exception
634	  covers **CI deploy credentials only**. Runtime credentials, such as a k0s autoscaler's AWS access to
635	  add or remove nodes, live in the cluster, not in GitHub; they follow layer 1 (no static keys, a
636	  role attached to the machine; ⚠️ not researched for k0s, G1).
637	- **What runs in the deploy job (OD22, phase 1).** Approved code runs with a prod deploy role:
638	  the Pulumi program during preview and apply, Serverless plugins, and any install script.
639	  The risk stop sees resources, not SDK calls the program makes while it runs, so it cannot
640	  catch this (OD15). Three controls limit the damage instead [design]:
641	  - **one environment per kind of stack:** the IAM stack deploys from `production-iam`, every
642	    other stack from `production`; each has its own OIDC subject and roles, so a domain stack's
643	    job cannot obtain the IAM stack's role (layer 1; examples E3, E4);
644	  - **domain roles are bounded:** they create or change only `svc-*` roles carrying the fixed
645	    permissions boundary (layer 1);
646	  - **no install scripts:** `npm_config_ignore_scripts` is set for the whole deploy and preview
647	    job ("npm does not run scripts specified in package.json files", 📖 R9.1.13; whether this
648	    covers every dependency is ⚠️ until tested on the runner). Packages that need their script
649	    are listed in `tools/ci/allowed-install-scripts.txt`, an L3 path, and rebuilt one by one
650	    (`npm rebuild <pkg>`, 📖 R9.1.13). npm v11 also has an `allowScripts` policy (📖 R9.1.13),
651	    an alternative once the CI npm version is known.
652	
653	  What stays: malicious code inside one stack can still do what that stack's role allows. The
654	  separate preview role of OD15 stays on the phase-2 roadmap (item 2.9), because `pulumi up`
655	  runs the same program again with the apply role.
656	- **Side paths:** Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments and Serverless Dashboard providers reach AWS
657	  (📖 R4.4.9) outside the GitHub gate (⚠️ R4.4.9); not used for prod (⚠️ R4.6 #6).
658	- **Pinning:** workflow lockfile (`gh actions-lock`) or full SHA, enforced by the org policy "Require
659	  actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA" (availability on Team ⚠️); the lockfile does not pin reusable workflows, so
660	  the deploy workflow lives in the same repo (📖 R3.5.5; conclusion [design]).
661	- **CODEOWNERS** on `.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`,
662	  `.husky/`, `.gitmodules`, `.ripgreprc`, `.devcontainer/` (📖 R3.2.8; list ⚠️ R6.5 #5, R6.3.11), plus
663	  `.npmrc` (registry redirection) [design], the policy packs, the SCP code, the
664	  catalogue file and the risk-stop classifier `tools/risk-stop/` (OD14: the deploy runs it from the
665	  merged commit, so a domain-approved PR could otherwise switch it off), the install-script allowlist `tools/ci/` (OD22), the Identity Center stack (OD23), the k0s RBAC and API-server configuration (OD24), and the on-call schedule `oncall/` (OD27). This is the canonical L3 path list that layer 3 refers to. Not on it:
666	  `deploy-approvals/<stack>/`, owned by the stack's owners and the on-call group (OD8, OD9). The private plugin
667	  marketplace is a separate repo with its own, stricter rulesets: two approvals, protected release
668	  tags (OD26; examples E9b). CI validates the file, because
669	  invalid lines are skipped silently (📖 R3.2.7). A fail-safe default line (`*` → L3 owner team and
670	  on-call group) keeps new stacks and root files from being unowned, since an unowned file accepts
671	  an approval from any writer (examples finding 7) [design].
672	- **No privileged triggers with untrusted code** (`pull_request_target`, `workflow_run` + checkout,
673	  📖 R3.5.4).
674	- **Agent review:** an independent agent (not the one that made the change) may post an automated
675	  review as an extra check; it never counts as an approval (GĐ-11). It runs on every PR that
676	  touches `infra/**`, `policy-packs/**` or a `serverless.yml` (OD22), so the human approver of
677	  code that will run with a deploy role always has a second reading of it [design].
678	- **Agents in CI:** `claude-code-action` with a custom GitHub App limited to Contents, Issues, Pull
679	  requests (📖 R1.7.8), whose own credentials are listed in the S2 inventory (⚠️ G19); Anthropic workload identity federation, not a personal OAuth token (📖 R1.7.6);
680	  `--restricted` and explicit `--tools` (D3; passing it through `claude_args` unverified, ⚠️ research
681	  6.9.4 Q5); a managed-settings file on the runner, which also guards against mods (📖 R1.5.6; for
682	  federation auth ⚠️); MCP set fixed by CI because `.mcp.json` loads without a prompt in `-p` runs
683	  (📖 R1.3.5); never `environment: production` (⚠️ R3.6 #4). Hosted runners give `sudo` (📖 R3.5.1),
684	  so with `Bash` in `--tools` the runner file is advisory (⚠️ R3.5.1, R3.6 #4).
685	- **App-opened PRs:** a required check set by a dedicated GitHub App, pinned as its source (layer 3), confirms at least one approval by a
686	  human who did not trigger the run; counting approvals is not enough, since the app's own approval
687	  might count (⚠️ R3.3.4, R3.7 A3; 📖 R3.2.5).
688	- **Required checks (S10):** from phase 1, secret scanning, dependency check, SAST (products: G4);
689	  from phase 2, IAM Access Analyzer `check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and Pulumi policy packs
690	  (📖 R4.2.2). For Serverless stacks, Access Analyzer would check the IAM policies in the
691	  CloudFormation template that `serverless package` produces, against the deployed ones (⚠️ not
692	  researched); policy packs do not apply to them. Until phase 2, the only compensation for OD8 is
693	  the risk stop, which fires on every IAM change in the prod preview. A mandatory policy is only
694	  advisory during a preview while a value is still unknown (✅ `@pulumi/policy` 1.21.0 source,
695	  examples finding 23), so Access Analyzer is the preview-time IAM check; the policy-pack example
696	  (E10) also lists the routes it does not cover.
697	
698	**Audit evidence.** Workflows and lockfile in git, the secrets inventory and exception register (S2), audit-log events for secrets and Actions settings, and check results per PR; full register: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#register).
699	
700	**Cost / value.** One-time migration to OIDC and pinned actions; slower action updates. Compliance

705	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
706	
707	**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).
708	Some paths rely on process (below), so this is a target, not a guarantee. Other customer
709	personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
710	by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved, name one
711	tenant, are time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
712	from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic or masked (GĐ-14).
713	
714	**On Papaya's stack**
715	
716	- **Paths to PHI** (research 1.11.4 lists 17):
717	  - AWS stores: closed by identity, through `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role from
718	    phase 1 (existing broad read roles are removed) and the SCP from phase 2
719	    (layer 1); no Aurora credentials, no prod exec, no `lambda:InvokeFunction` for agent-usable roles
720	    [design; actions ⚠️ G13];
721	  - k0s logs/exec and GCP stores (L1, L11, L13): same principle, mechanism open (G1, G3);
722	  - tickets/chat via MCP, pasted text, internal admin pages, prod AI traces, fixtures, CI logs (L5,
723	    L8–L10, L12, L14): process and hygiene only;
724	  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
725	    Redaction lives in application code, so one approved PR that logs a whole event would put
726	    PHI in a log group the agent reads. A second layer outside the code (OD28) [design]:
727	    - a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy on every log group `ProdReadMetadata` reads, set
728	      **before** the group is opened, because masking applies at ingestion only; masked data is
729	      hidden "at all egress points, including CloudWatch Logs Insights" (📖 R9.2.7);
730	    - custom identifiers keyed on field names (national ID, HKID, bank account, diagnosis,
731	      insured name; examples E14), because AWS has no managed identifier for Vietnam, Thailand
732	      or Hong Kong (📖 R9.2.8); at most 10, each regex ≤ 200 characters (📖 R9.2.9);
733	    - no agent-usable role holds `logs:Unmask`, and none gets `CloudWatchLogsFullAccess`, which
734	      includes it (📖 R9.2.7; E6 test);
735	    - a required SAST rule against logging whole events or payload objects in the claims
736	      services' handlers (S10; product open, G4); a log-level change already stops at the risk
737	      stop (`logging` property), because debug output can carry PHI.
738	    Limit: field-name masking catches structured logs, not free text in a message. It is a second
739	    layer; code review and the SAST rule remain the first. Cost: $0.12 per GB scanned
740	    (📖 R9.2.10) and masked values while debugging.
741	- **Real-data request** [design]: tenant, purpose, store, window, agreement; approved by the data owner
742	  and an approver ≠ requester; JIT data-read role, 1 h. At night the data owner is not on call: the
743	  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day. This
744	  applies to non-PHI and PHI alike; for PHI the reader is still a human without an agent. Per-tenant scoping through session tags
745	  (📖 R2.1.8) is unresolved, because tags come from user attributes (⚠️).
746	  - **PHI:** a human reads in a terminal without an agent (process rule, layer 1); the agent gets a
747	    redacted summary. This
748	    narrows GĐ-9 because the agent stays outside PHI scope (research 1.9) and Team is not shown as
749	    BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if needed (research 1.9).
750	  - **Non-PHI personal data:** the agent may read it within the approved request (GĐ-9). Claim
751	    tables mix health, ID and bank data (research 1.11.4 L2), so a store that holds PHI is treated as
752	    PHI unless the agent reads a view or extract without PHI [design].
753	- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b):** never in an agent session raw; reproduce with synthetic
754	  documents, or de-identify first [design]. The document is PHI and an injection vector (research
755	  1.11.4 L6).
756	- **Injection** (these lower frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact): Manual by default (sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, layer 2); the auto-mode
757	  classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions and 5.7 % of 1,000 synthetic exfiltration
758	  attempts (📖 R6.3.5). Broad allowed domains such as `github.com` are a documented exfiltration path
759	  (📖 R6.3.7). The incident session has no WebFetch, likely no edit tools (layer 2), and runs outside
760	  the repo, but its Bash can still write locally and send data out through excluded
761	  commands (layer 2), including the SSO token cache; "no standing write, no PHI read" limits what
762	  the token opens, except during a JIT or data-read window (layer 2 mitigations). Shared knowledge
763	  goes in `CLAUDE.md` under review; auto memory is exempt from the protected-path rules unless `--restricted` (📖 R6.3.11, D3).
764	- **Tenants:** one tenant per data-read grant; a session that read one tenant's data does not post to
765	  shared places without review (⚠️ R6.5 #8, process). Logical separation in shared accounts is assumed
766	  (GĐ-3, unconfirmed).
767	- **Non-prod:** no prod copies (S11). A scan of non-prod stores runs at the start of phase 1 (tool:
768	  G4); a store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule (GĐ-14: until cleaned, non-prod follows the GĐ-9 data-read rule). Cost: until scanned, that store is
769	  not part of the free loop.
770	- **Local stores:** transcripts and memory hold what the agent read (research 1.11.4); set
771	  `cleanupPeriodDays` (30 in the HIPAA sample, 📖 R5.5.4; what it deletes ⚠️).
772	- **Cross-border (Vietnam example):** processing data collected in Vietnam on a platform abroad is a
773	  transfer (📖 R5.4.5); agent flows, including employee names in logs and transcripts, update the
774	  transfer impact assessment (⚠️ R5.7 #4, needs Papaya legal).
775	
776	**Audit evidence.** SCP/IAM text as the written access rule for sensitive data, real-data requests with the data-read role's CloudTrail events, and non-prod scan results; full register: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#register).
777	
778	**Cost / value.** Debugging with redacted and synthetic data; a request for the rare real-data read.
779	Compliance gets "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM for AWS stores (fully from phase 2;
780	actions ⚠️ G13) and by process
781	elsewhere, and a record per exception (S9).

785	## Layer 7 — Observability, audit, incident response and break-glass
786	
787	**Principle.** One tamper-evident evidence chain per prod change. One routed alert channel with a
788	named on-call, approvers included. Unapproved change is detected (drift, reconciliation). Break-glass
789	is approved before use, time-boxed and reconciled after.
790	
791	**On Papaya's stack**
792	
793	- **Audit stores:**
794	  - organization CloudTrail to a log-archive account with integrity validation (📖 R2.6.2, R2.6.4,
795	    R2.6.5); change records ≥ 6 years; raw-log retention for Papaya's compliance owner (⚠️ R5.7 #2).
796	    Data events only on PHI buckets, prod Lambda invoke and prod SQS (cost 📖 R2.6.3; selection
797	    ⚠️ R2.9 #5), which makes the archive
798	    PHI-bearing (⚠️ research 1.11.4 L15). CloudTrail Lake is closed to new customers (📖 R2.6.6);
799	  - **evidence bucket** (OD30) [design]: an S3 bucket in the log-archive account with Object Lock
800	    in compliance mode, 6 years, which nobody, root included, can shorten or delete (📖 R9.2.12;
801	    a new bucket, since enabling it on an existing one was not confirmed). From phase 1 a nightly
802	    workflow writes the last day's merged PRs with their reviews and check runs, and the logs and
803	    artifacts (`risk-summary`) of deploy runs, through a role that may only `PutObject`
804	    (examples E13). Actions keeps logs 90 days by default, at most 400 (📖 R9.1.8): set 400 as
805	    a buffer;
806	  - GitHub org audit log kept 180 days (📖 R3.5.6). Its REST API is documented for Enterprise
807	    Cloud, not Team (📖 R9.1.5), so an org owner exports it monthly from the UI (JSON) into the
808	    evidence bucket, a manual step in the monthly report (📖 R9.1.7);
809	  - **JIT and real-data request records** (OD30): an issue in a dedicated Linear team, from a
810	    template with required fields (command list or store, scope, tenant, reason, incident link,
811	    agreement); the approver approves by moving it to an "Approved" state. Linear's audit log is
812	    Enterprise-only and kept 90 days, and its CSV export has no field history (📖 R9.1.14), so a
813	    webhook receiver in the tooling account (the approval-gate app's) writes every change, with
814	    the previous values Linear sends, to the evidence bucket. Not Slack;
815	  - alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`, `environment.update_protection_rule`,
816	    `environment.remove_protection_rule`, `environment.delete`, `protected_branch.policy_override`
817	    (📖 R3.5.6, R3.1.4; selection ⚠️ R3.6 #1). UI changes to the branch policy may leave no event, and a
818	    deleted `production` environment comes back unprotected (⚠️ R3.1.4): a job compares live settings
819	    with an expected copy (G8);
820	  - Aurora SQL is likely invisible to CloudTrail (⚠️ R2.7.1): Database Activity Streams, alerts on
821	    lost-record events (📖 R2.7.2; Serverless v2 ⚠️), stream treated as PHI (⚠️ R2.7.3);
822	  - Claude Code OTel without prompt content (layer 2);
823	  - Kubernetes API audit log of prod k0s (OD24, layer 5); destination open (G1).
824	- **Change record [design]:** keyed by commit SHA or JIT request ID; links PR, approvals, run ID,
825	  preview and CloudTrail events. Monthly reconciliation: every prod write event matches a record
826	  approved before apply (S3). Actor: `onBehalfOf.userId` where present, else session name plus
827	  directory lookup (📖 R2.5.1; ⚠️ R2.5.3).
828	- **Drift [design]:** its own role, trusted only from a `drift` environment on `main`; it can read
829	  prod secrets in state, which is noted (⚠️ R4.6 #2). Scheduled `pulumi preview --refresh
830	  --expect-no-changes` or `pulumi refresh --preview-only` (📖 R4.1.1, R4.3.1, R4.3.2). On a DIY S3
831	  backend, preview needs state-write permission (📖 R4.3.3); whether a refresh preview writes more
832	  than locks is open (⚠️ R4.6 #2, G14). So either the drift role gets state write (and the same
833	  trust care as the deploy role), or Pulumi Cloud drift detection is used (📖 R4.3.2, Pro+). The
834	  latter runs on Pulumi Deployments, which holds credentials to prod, so it re-opens a side path that
835	  layer 5 excludes and needs the same trust narrowing and audit (📖 R4.4.9; ⚠️ R4.6 #6). CloudFormation
836	  drift detection, explicitly set properties only (📖 R4.4.6). No auto-remediation: it is an unreviewed
837	  `pulumi up --refresh` (📖 R4.3.2). Each finding gets an actor and a ticket.
838	- **On-call:** phase 1 delivers the named approver schedule (primary + backup engineers, 24/7), as
839	  decided in framing round 1, and, because of OD7, a minimal incident-responder schedule; the
840	  latter extends that decision. The primary approves; the backup steps in only if the primary is
841	  unavailable (OD2). On-call approvers only approve during their shift; the fix is written by an
842	  incident responder (OD7). Alert routing and the
843	  rest of on-call follow in phase 2 (tools: G5); in phase 1 the responder calls the approver by phone from the published schedule.
844	  The schedule is also an input of the approval-gate app (OD27): in phase 1 it is the file
845	  `oncall/schedule.yaml` (an L3 path) and open incidents are incident issues in Linear, created
846	  before the PR is linked. The monthly report lists every `incident` PR with its incident, approver
847	  and shift, and every approval the app flagged (layer 3).
848	- **Break-glass = JIT fallback** [design unless marked]:
849	
850	  | Step | Rule |
851	  |---|---|
852	  | When | Only during an incident (Options §9 Q2), when the PR path cannot be used: operation not in IaC and no runbook; GitHub/Actions down; pipeline broken. The approver refuses JIT for anything expressible in IaC while the pipeline works, and records why. Outside incidents, an operation not in IaC waits for IaC or a runbook. |
853	  | Request | Command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub. |
854	  | Approval | On-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant (Options §4b; OD7; backup rule OD2). |
855	  | Grant | `InfraOperator-<service>`; role session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4). Deleting the assignment likely stops only new sessions (⚠️ R2.4.2, R2.9 #3), so the real window can approach 2 h; ending the portal session does not end role sessions (📖 R2.4.3). An immediate stop needs the revocation SCP, which must keep the user blocked for at least 12 h (📖 R2.4.4). Applying it is a management-account change held by the L3 owner team only, and no night-time path for it is designed yet (⚠️ G20): until one exists, a misused grant may run to the end of its window. Candidate: a pre-approved revocation runbook for one named L3 owner reachable by phone, or an org-wide `aws:TokenIssueTime` Deny as kill switch (⚠️ R2.9 #3). |
856	  | Execution | The grant goes to the requester (the incident responder), who types the commands; no agent in that terminal (D2). D2 said the on-call person runs them; OD7 moves that to the responder, since on-call engineers only approve. |
857	  | After | A job compares CloudTrail writes in the window with the list; a codify PR within a fixed deadline (as soon as GitHub is back); drift detection until it merges. |
858	  | Identity Center outage | Emergency SAML federation to roles, built and tested in advance (📖 R2.1.11; ⚠️ R2.9 #2); no user mapped until an approved activation, which is alerted. |
859	
860	  **Example request (illustrative command ⚠️):** "INC-123, ECS service `claims-api`, Actions outage. Run
861	  `aws ecs update-service --cluster <prod-cluster> --service <svc> --force-new-deployment`. Scope
862	  `InfraOperator-claims`, 1 h."
863	
864	  **Metrics** (Options §7; starting thresholds ⚠️ to calibrate): JIT used where a PR was possible
865	  (review at 1); writes outside the list (review at 1); codify PRs late (review at 1); grants per
866	  month and share of incidents needing non-IaC operations (review above about 25 %, a value new in
867	  this draft). On a breach,
868	  make the PR lane faster or add a runbook; do not widen JIT.
869	- **Roadmap:** runbooks for repeated non-IaC operations, if SSM Automation's approval step meets three
870	  conditions (Options §2; outside 02-research, G6); break-glass from an environment without the agent
871	  (D2, ⚠️).
872	
873	**Audit evidence.** Validated CloudTrail, the exported GitHub audit log, change records and monthly reconciliation (S3, S8), JIT records, drift tickets and incident approval waits (S7); full register: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#register).
874	
875	**Cost / value.** The incident lane is slower than direct access (estimated 11–46 vs 2–20 min,
876	Options §6), and JIT needs a written command list. Compliance gets approval before apply even in
877	incidents, plus detection.
878	
879	---
880	
881	## Layer 8 — Governance and rollout
882	
883	**Principle.** Every control has an owner, a metric and a review date. Policies are files changed by
884	PR. Access is never removed before its replacement works. Controls are tested against realistic
885	attacks.
886	
887	**On Papaya's stack**
888	
889	- **Owners:** DevSecOps (framework, managed settings, catalogue, metrics); a platform team or named
890	  engineers (deploy workflows, rulesets, pipelines; whether Papaya has a platform team is unknown ⚠️); Compliance (evidence review, supplier register, Statement of
891	  Applicability); engineering leads (decide CODEOWNERS content; changes to it are approved by the L3 owner team); engineering management (on-call schedule).
892	- **Policy as code:** catalogue, SCPs, trust policies, CODEOWNERS and workflows are files under
893	  CODEOWNERS. Settings that live outside files are kept as an expected copy in git and compared with
894	  the live state: GitHub settings (⚠️ R3.6 #1; G8) and Claude managed settings, which are edited in
895	  the admin console (📖 R1.1.5; comparison method in layer 2). Few GitHub admins and Claude org
896	  Owners, reviewed quarterly.
897	- **Metrics:** S1–S11 exactly as in framing §5; this framework adds the JIT metrics (layer 7) and the
898	  prompt metrics (layer 2). S2 and S5 have caveats (OD1; layer 2).
899	- **Rollout** (≈ 90 days, GĐ-12 unconfirmed): [`03-rollout-plan.md`](03-rollout-plan.md), moved
900	  there with its items unchanged except syncs with the examples' findings (trail deny, allowlist,
901	  phase-2 version floor), and expanded with owners and checks [design]. Order (framing Q8): (1) remove long-lived CI credentials, (2) narrow standing prod
902	  access, (3) MCP/plugin catalogue; the on-call approver list before or with (2). Phase 1 (0–30 days)
903	  makes the PR the default prod write path, with six hard prerequisites before standing prod write is
904	  removed; phase 2 (30–60) adds SCPs, the rest of the managed baseline and automated
905	  reconciliation; phase 3 (60–90) tests and reviews. The phase-1 load on 1–2 DevSecOps people is the
906	  main rollout risk [design; effort not estimated ⚠️].
907	
908	- **Exceptions:** a ticket with owner, reason and expiry.
909	- **Standards mapping:** ISO 27001:2022 Annex A (IDs recalled, ⚠️ R5.1), HIPAA Security Rule
910	  (📖 R5.2) and Vietnam law (📖 R5.4) are mapped per control area in the
911	  [compliance register](04-compliance-mapping.md#standards-cross-reference), with every caveat. "A named human approves"
912	  is Papaya's chosen way to meet these controls, not a literal requirement (⚠️ R5.7 #1).
913	- **Out of scope:** security of the production AI agents (A7a); noted as a follow-up.
914	
915	**Audit evidence.** Git history of policy files, monthly metrics, 90-day review minutes, the exception register and planted-injection reports; standards: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#standards-cross-reference).
916	
917	**Cost / value.** Steady, small overhead for DevSecOps and the owners of deploy workflows. Compliance gets a managed system
918	with owners and review dates.
919	
920	---
921	
922	## Gaps (not covered, or only as an open item, in `work/02-research.md`)
923	
924	| # | Gap | Layers |
925	|---|---|---|
926	| G1 | k0s: human authentication and RBAC (GĐ-4); placing the audit policy on controllers and shipping the audit log; the target OIDC trust on Papaya's k0s version (OD24 gives interim controls); break-glass when Actions is down | 1, 3, 6, 7 |
927	| G2 | Firebase Hosting deploy from CI without a stored token; break-glass when Actions is down | 1, 5, 7 |
928	| G3 | Human and agent access to GCP (roles, data access) | 1, 6 |
929	| G4 | Secret scanning, dependency check, SAST, non-prod data scanning on the Team plan | 5, 6 |
930	| G5 | Paging and alert routing; approving a PR from a phone | 7 |
931	| G6 | SSM Automation `aws:approve` (read in `work/03-options.md` §2, not in 02-research) | 7 |
932	| G7 | GitHub Actions log and artifact retention, and export | 3, 7 |
933	| G8 | Rulesets and environment settings through the API | 7, 8 |
934	| G9 | How Linear and Slack MCP servers authenticate | 4, 6 |
935	| G10 | OIDC subject customisation (`job_workflow_ref`) on GitHub Team | 1 |
936	| G11 | Closing provider/login bypasses on laptops without MDM | 2 |
937	| G12 | `pulumi up` flag reference for the prod allowlist | 3 |
938	| G13 | IAM actions for every data-plane read (S3, SQS, Step Functions, Secrets Manager, RDS, ECS Exec, Lambda invoke) | 1, 6 |
939	| G14 | Which state writes a Pulumi refresh preview needs on a DIY S3 backend | 3, 7 |
940	| G15 | Restricting a self-hosted runner to one workflow in a monorepo; just-in-time runners | 5 |
941	| G16 | Managing GitHub team membership as code; audit event for a membership change | 3, 7 |
942	| G17 | Who forms the L3 owner team and how many people (GĐ-1: never a single reviewer) | 3, 8 |
943	| G18 | Reading the live values of server-managed settings (API or local cache) to compare with git | 2, 8 |
944	| G19 | Required-check app and CI-agent app: review-event triggers, source pinning against same-name checks, hosting, private-key storage and whether those keys count against S2; the app's check that a risk-stop approval matches the stopped run's hash (OD18); reading Linear incidents and the schedule (OD27). The decision logic itself is examples E12 | 3, 5 |
945	| G20 | Emergency revocation at night: who can apply the revocation Deny SCP (management account) within minutes; `aws:TokenIssueTime` kill switch (⚠️ R2.9 #3) | 1, 7 |
946	
947	Open checks from `work/03-options.md` §8 remain open.
948	
949	## Owner decisions (2026-11-09)
950	
951	The owner answered the open questions of draft v3. English rendering; the original Vietnamese
952	answers are recorded in `work/session-log.md`.
953	
954	| # | Question | Decision |
955	|---|---|---|
956	| OD1 | Exception to S2 = 0 for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials? | Yes, provided each credential has a single source of truth. (The first reason given, continuous scale-in/scale-out, concerns runtime credentials; OD6 narrowed the scope.) |
957	| OD2 | L3: must one approver be from the platform team? | Not necessarily; one approval procedure is agreed for all engineers, and the on-call engineer is enough. Clarified in follow-ups: every change involves two people, one who makes it and one who approves; the on-call backup only replaces an unavailable primary. Asked whether L3 should need more approvers than L2, the owner chose "L3 = 1 approver at all times"; in the agent's framing of that option, the approver must own the path. |
958	| OD3 | `CLAUDE.md` changes: L2 or L3? | L3, because the workflow must be consistent across the whole team. |
959	| OD4 | Move the rest of the managed baseline and the SSM check to phase 2? | Yes. |
960	| OD5 | "An agent does not approve PRs" only a process rule? | It is a rule: the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent. |
961	| OD6 | Scope of OD1: CI deploy credentials only, or also runtime scaling credentials? | CI deploy credentials (k0s kubeconfig/token, Firebase token in GitHub secrets) only, until it is checked whether k0s and Firebase can use OIDC. |
962	| OD7 | (a) If the on-call engineer writes an L3 fix, who approves? (b) Keep the read-only allowlist in phase 1? | (a) "While on call, never change the process"; clarified: on-call engineers only approve, and fixes are written by another engineer (the incident responder), so the approver is never the author. (b) Yes, as proposed. |
963	| OD8 | IAM/network/stateful changes inside a domain file: who approves the risk stop? | The stack's owners (may be the first approver); always two people. The L3 owner team keeps only the real L3 paths; Access Analyzer and policy packs compensate. |
964	| OD9 | How can one on-call primary approve any path at night? | The on-call approver group co-owns every deployable path; one primary + one backup. Normal-day domain review is a process rule with a monthly check. |
965	| OD10 | A PR touching files of several domain teams: split, or one approval? | One approval is enough (two-person rule kept); domain review on such PRs is a recommendation, counted in the monthly report. |
966	| OD11 | Risk stop when the first approver is unavailable: may another owner of the stack approve? | Yes; it makes three people and is recorded as a deviation. |
967	| OD12 | `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed`: `true` or `false`? | Keep `true` (fewer prompts, relies on the sandbox, which arrives in phase 2). |
968	| OD13 | Confirm three agent readings: (1) OD8, who opens and approves the risk-stop approval PR; (2) OD9, scope of the on-call group; (3) L3-JIT, does the on-call approver count as service owner? | Confirmed: (1) the original author opens it and the first approver approves it; (2) the on-call group does not co-own process-defining paths or the SCP stack, which only the L3 owner team approves; (3) yes. |
969	| OD14 | Add the risk-stop classifier (`tools/risk-stop/`) to the canonical L3 path list? (found while writing `examples/`) | Yes: it is a control, so only the L3 owner team may change it. |
970	| OD15 | Scope of the risk stop: risky diffs nobody looked at, or also malicious approved code? | Keep the current scope and state its limits; a separate prod preview role and a job split go to the phase-2 roadmap. |
971	| OD16 | Squash-only merges to `main` (needed so a PR cannot carry its own risk-stop approval)? | Yes; the cost is that PR-internal commit history is not kept on `main`. |
972	| OD17 | Deploy only the current tip of `main`, so re-running an old run cannot roll prod back? | Yes; added to the layer-3 "merge approval = deploy approval" conditions. |
973	| OD18 | An approval merged before a deploy stops, matched by a later change outside the stack's directory, is still accepted | Accepted as a stated limit; the approval-gate app (G19) is to close it by checking the stopped run's hash. |
974	| OD19 | Protect the names of SCP-exempt roles (`app-claims-*`, `cfn-deployment-*`, `github-prod-deploy-*`) so that only the IAM stack's deploy role can create or change them? (found while writing `examples/`) | Yes. Confirmed reading: "only the IAM stack" holds once OD20 gives the IAM stack its own role and OIDC subject; until then the protection is "only an approved prod Pulumi deploy". OD22 gives the IAM stack that role and subject in phase 1. |
975	| OD20 | Code in the deploy job (install scripts, Pulumi program, Serverless plugins) can request the job's OIDC token for either prod deploy role: fix now or roadmap? | Roadmap phase 2, together with OD15: a build job without `id-token`, and per-role environments (different OIDC subjects) or `job_workflow_ref`. Until then it is a stated limit. **Superseded in timing by OD22:** per-environment roles move to phase 1. |
976	| OD21 | Phase 1 lets built-in read-only commands (`cat`, `head` …) read `~/.aws` without a prompt, and allow rules skip the auto-mode classifier: add keys to the phase-1 subset? | Yes: add a `Read(~/.aws/**)` deny rule and `autoMode.classifyAllShell: true` (examples finding 19). |
977	
978	**Fixes after the independent review** (`work/07-review.md`; proposals and the owner's choices in
979	`work/08-fix-proposals.md`, documentation checks in `work/09-fix-research.md`). The owner accepted
980	every proposal on 2026-11-09:
981	
982	| # | Review finding | Decision |
983	|---|---|---|
984	| OD22 | Approved code runs with a prod deploy role, which can change SCP-exempt roles (review A-1) | Moves OD20 into phase 1: the IAM stack gets its own environment `production-iam` and role; domain deploy roles change only `svc-*` roles under a fixed permissions boundary; no install scripts in deploy and preview jobs except a reviewed allowlist (L3 path); agent review on every PR touching infrastructure code. The separate preview role (OD15) stays in phase 2. |
985	| OD23 | Identity Center administrators and `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` can grant prod write outside the design (review C-4) | Identity Center permission sets and assignments as code (L3 owner team only) with alerts on other changes; an SCP denies `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` in the prod OU; member-account root credentials removed; a named management-account group. |
986	| OD24 | The long-lived k0s deploy credential is undetectable if leaked, on the cluster that runs AI agents reading partner documents (review A-4) | Phase 1: a namespaced, time-limited ServiceAccount token without Secret, exec, log, token, RBAC or delete rights; `production-k0s` environment required; Kubernetes API audit log. Target: k0s trusts GitHub OIDC directly. |
987	| OD25 | An approval proves a GitHub account, not a named person; an agent can approve through its engineer's login (review C-1) | Required 2FA, a login register fed by HR with quarterly review, restricted personal access tokens; from phase 1, managed deny rules for `gh pr review`, `gh api …reviews…` and the `gh` token file (hygiene); Enterprise Cloud (SAML, environment reviewers, audit-log streaming) is listed with its price as a decision for Papaya. |
988	| OD26 | A component that runs on every laptop (plugin, hook, local MCP server) can give an attacker many logins at once, so author ≠ approver is no longer two independent people (review A-2, A-3) | Threat T23; marketplace pinned to a protected release tag, every plugin (internal too) pinned by `sha`, auto-update off; local MCP servers only as immutable artifacts (image digest or pinned plugin); approval-gate app flags suspicious approvals; **process paths need two L3 owner team members** (partly reverses OD2, ADR-0012). |
989	| OD27 | The `incident` label opens cross-domain approval, and anyone with Triage can apply it (review E-2) | The approval-gate app counts an on-call approval for another team's file only with an open incident and the approver on shift; the label alone grants nothing; every `incident` PR is in the monthly report. Consequence: on normal days a cross-team PR needs an owner of each team (changes the effect of OD10; ADR-0012). The app becomes a hard phase-1 prerequisite. |
990	| OD28 | PHI could reach the agent through a log group it may read, if one approved PR logs a whole event (review A-1b) | CloudWatch Logs masking with custom identifiers on those log groups, set before they open; no `logs:Unmask` for agent-usable roles; a SAST rule against logging whole events. Stated as a second layer: AWS has no managed identifiers for VN/TH/HK. |
991	| OD29 | No designed path for schema migrations and data fixes (review E-1) | `sql` job of the deploy workflow with its own database role (IAM auth), SQL risk stop, metadata changes always stop, data fixes per tenant with expected rows and a data owner's approval (L3-data-write); ADR-0011. A hard prerequisite of removing standing prod write. |
992	| OD30 | Evidence before phase 2 can expire; JIT and data-read approvals have no store (review C-2, C-3) | From phase 1: evidence bucket with Object Lock (compliance, 6 years), nightly export of PRs, reviews, checks, deploy logs and artifacts; monthly manual export of the org audit log; Linear template for JIT and data-read requests, mirrored to the bucket by webhook. Closes O-1 and O-4. |

1	# Engineer guide: working with Claude Code at Papaya
     2	
     3	> Status: a summary of the approved framework; it adds no rule · Updated: 2026-11-09 · Builds on
     4	> [`01-framework.md`](01-framework.md)
     5	
     6	This page answers one question: **what changes in my working day?** Each section says what you do,
     7	who approves, and how long it takes. The rules and their sources are in the framework layer linked
     8	from each section; if this page and the framework differ, the framework wins. Times are targets from
     9	the success criteria (S-n) or estimates marked ⚠️.
    10	
    11	## The short version
    12	
    13	- **Non-prod is yours.** Build, deploy and debug in non-prod with the agent, with no new approval (S4),
    14	  once a store has been scanned for real data (until then it follows the real-data rule, section 5).
    15	- **Prod reads are metrics and metadata.** No standing prod write for anyone, you included.
    16	- **Every prod change is a pull request.** One code owner who is not you approves; CI applies it.
    17	- **In an incident the path is the same, with faster people:** an on-call approver, 24/7.
    18	- **Real customer data, new tools and break-glass need a request.** Each has a named approver and a time limit.
    19	
    20	## 1. Daily development (non-prod)
    21	
    22	- **What you do:** use Claude Code as you do today, with non-prod roles. Manual permission mode is the
    23	  default; you may switch to auto mode (D1). Commands that run inside the sandbox run without a prompt
    24	  (phase 2, OD12).
    25	- **Approval:** none (risk level L1).
    26	- **What is different:** the organisation's managed settings apply to everyone; bypass mode is
    27	  removed; plugins and MCP servers come from the catalogue only (section 6). From phase 2 the sandbox
    28	  hides credentials and blocks Unix sockets, so `git push`, `gh`, Docker and private-registry `npm ci` fail inside it: run
    29	  them yourself at the `!` prompt. Using `--restricted` is recommended (D3).
    30	- **From phase 2 you will also notice** (layer 2, examples E8): each `aws`, `pulumi` or `serverless`
    31	  call asks you first, in auto mode too; each WebFetch asks; your own and the project's permission
    32	  rules are ignored, so prompts may rise; sign-in is locked to Papaya's organisation (API-key sessions
    33	  are refused) and the minimum Claude Code version rises; on macOS, servers on localhost fail inside
    34	  the sandbox; native Windows is not supported (use WSL2).
    35	- **Layer:** [2](01-framework.md#layer-2--agent-runtime-controls).
    36	
    37	## 2. Reading prod
    38	
    39	- **What you do:** with `ProdReadMetadata` (1-hour session) you and your agent read metrics, metadata
    40	  and logs that are redacted at source and masked by a data protection policy (OD28): identifiers
    41	  such as national IDs, bank accounts and diagnoses show as masked values. Lambda configuration is readable per service once its secrets
    42	  are resolved at runtime; until then, read timeout and memory from the IaC code.
    43	- **Approval:** none (L0).
    44	- **Cost to know:** in the first months, raw logs of services not yet redacted are not readable
    45	  without a data-read request (section 5). This is the largest cost of the transition.
    46	- **Remember:** the agent uses **your** AWS SSO session, so it can do whatever you can (layer 1). Keep
    47	  the portal session short.
    48	- **Layer:** [1](01-framework.md#layer-1--identity-and-access).
    49	
    50	## 3. Shipping a prod change
    51	
    52	1. Write the change as code (Pulumi, `serverless.yml`, Kubernetes manifests) and preview it on non-prod.
    53	2. Push the branch and open a pull request. The PR runs secret scanning, dependency checks and SAST
    54	   (S10), and previews non-prod only.
    55	3. One code owner of the changed files approves. You cannot approve your own PR, and the approver may
    56	   not be the last person who pushed. An agent never approves a PR (OD5); managed settings also
    57	   block `gh pr review` for agents (OD25).
    58	   - Domain code and stacks: your domain team. Members of the on-call group are co-owners, but
    59	     their approval counts for another team's files only on an incident PR while they are on shift;
    60	     the approval-gate check enforces it (OD27). A PR that touches several teams' files needs an
    61	     owner of each.
    62	   - Process files (`.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/`, the catalogue, the SCP stack,
    63	     `tools/risk-stop/`, `tools/ci/`, `oncall/`): **two** members of the L3 owner team (OD26).
    64	4. Merge (squash only). The deploy job previews prod and applies the change.
    65	5. **If the deploy stops at the risk stop** (stateful replace or delete, IAM, network, a policy
    66	   finding): open a second PR that adds only `deploy-approvals/<stack>/<stopped commit>.yaml` with the
    67	   hash from the job summary. By default the first approver approves it; if they are unavailable,
    68	   another owner of the stack does, which is recorded as a deviation (OD13, OD11). Merging it deploys
    69	   if the new prod preview has the same hash. While the stack is stopped, later merges to it stop too.
    70	
    71	- **Time:** same working day from PR to prod; approval wait ≤ 1 hour in working hours (S4 targets).
    72	- **What CI does differently (OD22):** npm install scripts do not run in preview and deploy jobs;
    73	  if a package needs its script, ask the L3 owner team to add it to `tools/ci/allowed-install-scripts.txt`.
    74	  A stack may create IAM roles for its own services only as `svc-*` roles with the standard
    75	  permissions boundary; roles that read claim data (`app-claims-*`) are created in the IAM stack
    76	  and referenced by ARN. PRs that touch infrastructure code also get an automated agent review,
    77	  which is advice, not an approval.
    78	- **Layer:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level); diagram
    79	  [`01-change-workflow`](../diagrams/01-change-workflow.svg).
    80	
    81	## 3a. Database changes and data fixes
    82	
    83	- **Schema and metadata:** write the migration (or GraphQL-engine metadata change) as a file under
    84	  `db/<service>/`, open a PR, get your domain owner's approval as for code. After merge the `sql`
    85	  deploy job applies it with its own database role; nobody, you included, holds database
    86	  credentials (OD29, ADR-0011).
    87	- **Data fix** (a stuck claim, a payout to retry): a file `db/<service>/data-fixes/<tenant>/<ticket>.sql`
    88	  for one tenant, with a `-- expected_rows: N` header. It needs a code owner **and** a different
    89	  person from that tenant's data owners (L3-data-write). The job rolls it back if the row count
    90	  differs, and its summary shows counts only.
    91	- **Expect a stop** for `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, column type changes, `DELETE`/`UPDATE` without a
    92	  `WHERE`, grants and row-level security, and every metadata change: open the
    93	  `deploy-approvals/` PR as in step 5 above. Prefer expand/contract migrations.
    94	- **In an incident:** the same path; the on-call approver may stand in for the data owner, who
    95	  reviews it the next working day.
    96	- **Layer:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level).
    97	
    98	## 4. An incident at 2 a.m.
    99	
   100	You are the **incident responder**. The **on-call approver** only approves; they never write the fix (OD7).
   101	
   102	1. Start an incident-analysis session with read-only roles, in an empty scratch directory outside
   103	   the repository: `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"` (no WebFetch; Bash can still reach
   104	   the network). Read metrics and redacted logs.
   105	2. Open (or find) the incident issue in Linear. Make the fix in a normal session, preview on
   106	   non-prod, and open a PR labelled `incident` that links the issue: the on-call approval counts
   107	   only while the issue is open and the approver is on shift (OD27).
   108	3. Call the on-call approver (phone in phase 1; routed alerts from phase 2). They review and approve.
   109	   If they find a problem, you push the fix and they approve again.
   110	4. Merge; the deploy job applies the change.
   111	
   112	- **Time:** target ≤ 15 min waiting for approval (S7); 11–46 min from decision to apply is an
   113	  estimate (⚠️), measured first during rollout against a 30-minute target.
   114	- **Blockers to know:** a risky change already waiting on `main` blocks your fix for that stack until
   115	  it is approved or reverted; at night, process files (workflows, `CLAUDE.md`, catalogue) wait for the
   116	  L3 owner team, or the JIT fallback applies.
   117	- **Only if the PR path cannot be used** (GitHub Actions down, broken pipeline, an operation not in
   118	  IaC): end your AWS portal session and sign in fresh, then open a JIT request issue in Linear from
   119	  its template (outside GitHub), with the exact commands; it is the record of the request (OD30). The on-call approver approves before the grant.
   120	  You get `InfraOperator-<service>` (1-hour role session; the real window can approach 2 h) and type
   121	  the commands yourself, in a terminal **without an agent**. Afterwards your commands are compared
   122	  with CloudTrail (by hand in phase 1, by a job from phase 2), and you open a PR that codifies the change.
   123	- **Layers:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level),
   124	  [7](01-framework.md#layer-7--observability-audit-incident-response-and-break-glass); diagram
   125	  [`03-incident-lane`](../diagrams/03-incident-lane.svg).
   126	
   127	## 5. Reading real customer data
   128	
   129	- **What you do:** end your AWS portal session and sign in fresh, then open a data-read request issue
   130	  in Linear from its template, with one tenant, purpose, store, time window and the agreement that
   131	  covers it (OD30). You get a data-read role for 1 hour.
   132	  After reading one tenant's data, do not post to shared places without review.
   133	- **Approval:** an approver who is not you, plus the data owner. At night the on-call approver
   134	  approves alone, and the data owner reviews it the next working day.
   135	- **PHI (medical records):** you read it yourself, in a terminal **without an agent**; give the agent
   136	  only a redacted summary. A store that holds PHI counts as PHI unless the agent reads a view without
   137	  it. Partner-uploaded claim documents never go into an agent session raw: reproduce with synthetic
   138	  documents, or de-identify them first.
   139	- **Non-prod** should hold no real data; a store not yet scanned follows this section's rule.
   140	- **Layer:** [6](01-framework.md#layer-6--data-protection-and-prompt-injection-defence).
   141	
   142	## 6. Adding a plugin or MCP server
   143	
   144	- **What you do:** open a request with what the tool reads, where it sends data and which write
   145	  tools it needs. A local MCP server is admitted only as a container image pinned by digest or as
   146	  code inside a pinned plugin, not as `npx -y <package>` (OD26). Keep your GitHub CLI token in the
   147	  system credential store (`gh auth status` shows where it is). A catalogue entry is added by a PR with a review record (examples
   148	  [`reviews/`](../examples/claude/marketplace/reviews/)).
   149	- **Approval:** two members of the L3 owner team (the catalogue is a process path, OD26).
   150	- **Time:** decided within 5 working days (S6).
   151	- **Not allowed:** installing a plugin or MCP server outside the catalogue, or sideloading one with
   152	  command-line flags.
   153	- **Layer:** [4](01-framework.md#layer-4--supply-chain-for-mcp-servers-and-plugins).
   154	
   155	## 7. When you are the on-call approver
   156	
   157	- You are on a named 24/7 schedule: a primary and a backup. The primary approves; the backup steps in
   158	  only if the primary is unavailable (OD2).
   159	- While on call you **only approve**: you do not write fixes or request JIT grants (OD7). A night
   160	  incident therefore needs two people awake: the responder and you.
   161	- Target: approve within 15 minutes (S7). Approve JIT only when the PR path cannot be used, and record
   162	  why you refuse it otherwise.
   163	- Approve another domain's PR only if it is labelled `incident`, links an open incident, and you
   164	  are on shift (OD9, OD27); the approval-gate check does not count it otherwise.
   165	- **Layers:** [3](01-framework.md#layer-3--change-workflow-by-risk-level),
   166	  [7](01-framework.md#layer-7--observability-audit-incident-response-and-break-glass).
   167	
   168	## 8. Shared agent knowledge
   169	
   170	`CLAUDE.md` and other agent configuration files define how the whole team works, so changes to them
   171	are approved by two members of the L3 owner team; a domain-team approval does not count (OD3, OD26). Review your agent's auto memory
   172	and delete it after a suspicious session (D3).
   173	
   174	## Where the evidence comes from
   175	
   176	You do not write separate evidence: the PR, its approvals, the deploy run and CloudTrail form the
   177	record of every prod change. Compliance's view is in
   178	[`04-compliance-mapping.md`](04-compliance-mapping.md).

=== 0003-merge-to-main-is-the-approval-gate.md
     1	# ADR-0003: The merge to `main` is the approval gate: two people, code owners, on-call co-ownership
     2	
     3	- **Status:** Accepted
     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-5, GĐ-8, GĐ-11; OD2, OD5, OD7, OD9, OD10, OD13)
     6	- **Scope:** GitHub monorepo rulesets, CODEOWNERS, `production` environment, on-call schedule
     7	
     8	## 1. Context
     9	
    10	Papaya is assumed to be on GitHub Team (GĐ-5), where environment required reviewers do not exist for
    11	private repositories (📖 R3.1.2), so the approval must happen before the deploy job. Incidents need an
    12	approver within 15 minutes, 24/7 (S7), and code-owner review requires an approval from an owner of the files (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.7;
    13	per-file behaviour ⚠️).
    14	
    15	## 2. Options considered
    16	
    17	| Option | Pros | Cons |
    18	|---|---|---|
    19	| A. Upgrade to Enterprise for environment reviewers | Approval sits next to the deploy | Cost; not assumed (GĐ-5) |
    20	| B. Merge to `main` as the gate; `production` limited to `main` | Works on Team; the approver sees the code that will be applied | Nobody sees the prod diff before apply (partly handled by ADR-0004) |
    21	| C. More approvers for high-risk changes | More eyes | Slower; the owner wants two people per change |
    22	
    23	## 3. Decision
    24	
    25	Option B. Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
    26	approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
    27	push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5); branch up to date, since there is no merge queue
    28	(⚠️ R4.6 #1). `production` accepts only `main` (📖 R3.1.3).
    29	
    30	- **Merge = deploy approval** only if the reusable deploy workflow alone references `production`,
    31	  with no ref/SHA inputs, no `issue_comment`, `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` triggers, one
    32	  concurrency group per stack without `cancel-in-progress` (📖 R4.1.4; ⚠️ R3.6 #1, from 📖 R3.1.3, R3.4.5c).
    33	- **Two people per change:** one makes it, one approves it; the approver is always an engineer,
    34	  never an agent (OD2, OD5). L3 changes need one approver too, who must own the path.
    35	- **Incidents:** on-call engineers only approve; an incident responder writes the fix (OD7).
    36	- **Night coverage:** an on-call approver group co-owns every deployable path in CODEOWNERS; one
    37	  primary, one backup (OD9). It does not co-own process-defining paths (`.github/**`, CODEOWNERS,
    38	  agent config, catalogue) or the SCP stack, which only the L3 owner team approves (OD13); IAM-only
    39	  stacks are deployable, so it co-owns them with the L3 owner team.
    40	- **Agent review:** an independent agent may post an automated review; it never counts as an
    41	  approval (GĐ-11).
    42	- **Cross-team PRs:** one approval is enough (OD10).
    43	
    44	## 4. Consequences
    45	
    46	- **Positive:** four-eyes enforced by GitHub, not by the agent; one rule for normal days and incidents.
    47	- **Negative / trade-offs:** GitHub accepts an approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so the
    48	  on-call group can approve another domain's PR; domain review on normal days is a process rule.
    49	- **Risks & how we watch them:** admins can edit the gate, logged, not prevented (⚠️ R3.2.2, R3.6 #1;
    50	  logging 📖 R3.2.2); alerts on ruleset changes; monthly report of cross-domain approvals. An agent could approve through its engineer's login; no detection found (⚠️). The
    51	  required-check app's hosting, key and triggers are open (⚠️ G19).
    52	- **Next steps:** rulesets, CODEOWNERS and its validation check in phase 1; the required-check app
    53	  before any agent workflow may open PRs; L3 owner team composition open (G17).
    54	
    55	## 5. References
    56	
    57	- Framework layer 3 ("Gate = merge to `main`", "Who approves at night"), layer 7 (audit alerts).
    58	- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004.
=== 0010-risk-level-decides-who-approves.md
     1	# ADR-0010: Risk level decides who approves, not how many; non-prod needs no approval
     2	
     3	- **Status:** Accepted
     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission (GĐ-14; OD2, OD3, OD8, OD9, OD13)
     6	- **Scope:** every change made by engineers and their agents, from non-prod to production
     7	
     8	## 1. Context
     9	
    10	Engineering says "Let Claude Code talk to AWS directly" (brief); the need is speed. Compliance's
    11	sentence covers production writes only (framing §3.1). A single rule for all changes either slows non-prod for
    12	no gain or leaves high-risk prod changes with too light a review. The owner also wants every prod
    13	change to need two people, no more by default: one who makes it and one who approves it (OD2).
    14	
    15	## 2. Options considered
    16	
    17	| Option | Pros | Cons |
    18	|---|---|---|
    19	| A. Same approval for everything | Simple | Non-prod loop slowed for no gain; high-risk changes get no extra scrutiny |
    20	| B. More approvers as risk grows (e.g. two for L3) | More eyes on dangerous changes | Breaks the two-person rule; slower incidents |
    21	| C. Risk level narrows who may approve, plus a risk stop; non-prod free | Fast where damage is small; specialist owners where it is large | One reviewer for high-risk changes can miss things |
    22	
    23	## 3. Decision
    24	
    25	Option C [design levels]:
    26	
    27	| Level | What | Approval |
    28	|---|---|---|
    29	| L0 | Reads: non-prod anything, prod metadata | none |
    30	| L1 | Changes in non-prod (synthetic or masked data only, GĐ-14) | none, author only |
    31	| L2 | Routine prod change, e.g. Lambda memory 1024 → 2048 MB | 1 code owner ≠ author, ≠ last pusher |
    32	| L3 | IAM/SCP, stateful replace/delete, network, workflow and agent-config files, catalogue, advisory policy finding (full list: framework layer 5) | 1 owner of that path |
    33	| L3-JIT | Break-glass in an incident | on-call approver ≠ requester (ADR-0005) |
    34	| L3-data | Real customer data read | approver ≠ requester + agreement; data-owner co-approval [design] (ADR-0009) |
    35	
    36	`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent-configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for the
    37	whole team (OD3). Process-defining paths and the SCP stack are owned by the L3 owner team; IAM or
    38	stateful changes inside a domain file are approved by that stack's owners (OD8, OD13). At every level,
    39	the risk stop applies to any deploy whose prod diff is risky (ADR-0004).
    40	
    41	## 4. Consequences
    42	
    43	- **Positive:** a free non-prod loop for engineers and agents (S4); the same two-person rule for every
    44	  prod change, incidents included (three people only by recorded deviation, OD11). Compliance gets a written rule for who may approve what.
    45	- **Negative / trade-offs:** one approver for high-risk changes (owner's trade-off for speed);
    46	  `CLAUDE.md` edits wait for the L3 owner team, not the domain team that edits them most.
    47	- **Risks & how we watch them:** the free loop holds only if non-prod has no real data; a non-prod
    48	  store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule until scanned (S11). A risky diff hidden in an L2 PR is
    49	  caught by the risk stop, not by the level (Pulumi and Serverless stacks only;
    50	  k0s and Firebase have none yet, G1, G2).
    51	- **Next steps:** non-prod data scan and CODEOWNERS with the L3 path list in phase 1; composition of
    52	  the L3 owner team is open (G17).
    53	
    54	## 5. References
    55	
    56	- Framework layer 3 (levels table), layer 5 (canonical L3 path list), layer 6 (non-prod).
    57	- Related: ADR-0003, ADR-0004, ADR-0005, ADR-0009.
=== 0011-database-changes-through-the-pipeline.md
     1	# ADR-0011: Database schema changes and data fixes go through the pipeline like any prod change
     2	
     3	- **Status:** Accepted
     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission, after the independent review (`work/07-review.md`; OD29)
     6	- **Scope:** Aurora PostgreSQL schema migrations, GraphQL-engine (Hasura) metadata, and data fixes on prod
     7	
     8	## 1. Context
     9	
    10	"Every prod change is a pull request" (ADR-0001) had no designed path for the two most frequent
    11	prod changes of a claims platform on Aurora with a GraphQL engine: schema migrations and data fixes
    12	(a stuck claim, a payout to retry). Once standing prod write is removed (rollout 1.16), nobody has a
    13	legitimate way to run them, which invites a shared database account or an admin endpoint: the
    14	shortcut the framework exists to remove. Data fixes also touch one tenant's customer data, which
    15	layer 6 treats as L3-data. IAM database authentication is not logged by CloudTrail (📖 R9.2.11).
    16	
    17	## 2. Options considered
    18	
    19	| Option | Pros | Cons |
    20	|---|---|---|
    21	| A. JIT grant with `psql` for data fixes; migrations at app start | Fast; no new tooling | An approved command list, not an approved change (ADR-0005's weakness) for routine work; migrations run with the app's role |
    22	| B. Migration and data-fix files in the monorepo, applied by the deploy workflow with a database role of its own, behind the risk stop | Same gate, same evidence as every other change | A migration job and two wrapper scripts per migration tool; data fixes need two approvers |
    23	| C. A separate database change tool with its own approvals | Purpose-built | A second approval system outside GitHub; a side path (T20) |
    24	
    25	## 3. Decision
    26	
    27	Option B [design]:
    28	
    29	- **Files:** migrations, GraphQL-engine metadata and data fixes live under `db/<service>/`; data
    30	  fixes under `db/<service>/data-fixes/<tenant>/<ticket>.sql`, one tenant per file, with an
    31	  `-- expected_rows: N` header.
    32	- **Approval:** migrations and metadata as any deployable path (domain owner, on-call in an
    33	  incident). Data fixes are **L3-data-write**: a code owner plus a different person from that
    34	  tenant's data-owner team, checked by the approval-gate app (E12, rule R4); in an incident the
    35	  on-call approver stands in and the data owner reviews the next working day (layer 6).
    36	- **Apply:** a `sql` job of the deploy workflow lists the pending files, runs the risk stop on them
    37	  (`--tool sql`: DROP, TRUNCATE, column type changes, unscoped DELETE/UPDATE, grants, roles,
    38	  row-level security, COPY, function bodies and every metadata change stop for a stack owner's
    39	  approval), then applies exactly the classified files, each in its own transaction; a data fix
    40	  whose affected-row count differs from its header is rolled back.
    41	- **Credentials:** the job's OIDC role may only `rds-db:connect` as the migration database user
    42	  (📖 R9.2.11); no person holds database credentials.
    43	- **Evidence:** the PR, the job log and summary (statement kinds and row counts, never values),
    44	  the risk-stop record; database-side activity through Database Activity Streams (layer 7),
    45	  because IAM database authentication is not in CloudTrail.
    46	
    47	## 4. Consequences
    48	
    49	- **Positive:** the most common prod changes get the same gate and evidence chain as code; data
    50	  fixes are scoped to one tenant and approved by its data owner; no standing database access.
    51	- **Negative / trade-offs:** a data fix takes a PR, two approvals and a deploy run instead of a
    52	  `psql` session; the two `tools/db/` scripts must be written for Papaya's migration tool
    53	  (unknown here); the SQL classifier is a heuristic, not a parser (examples E7).
    54	- **Risks & how we watch them:** a destructive statement hidden in a form the heuristic does not
    55	  know (function bodies and `EXECUTE` already stop); a wrong `expected_rows` is caught only if the
    56	  count differs; long migrations hold locks (expand/contract recommended, not enforced).
    57	- **Next steps:** `tools/db/` wrappers and the migration role in phase 1, before standing prod write
    58	  is removed (rollout 1.23).
    59	
    60	## 5. References
    61	
    62	- Framework layer 3 ("Database changes"), layer 6 (L3-data), layer 7 (Database Activity Streams).
    63	- Examples E3 (`sql` job), E7 (SQL rules), E12 (rule R4).
    64	- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004, ADR-0009, ADR-0012.
=== 0012-approval-integrity-checked-by-the-gate-app.md
     1	# ADR-0012: Approval integrity is checked by the approval-gate app: two approvals on process paths, on-call approvals only for open incidents
     2	
     3	- **Status:** Accepted; supersedes in part ADR-0003 (domain review on normal days as a process rule; one approval for cross-team PRs, OD10) and ADR-0010 (one approver for L3 process paths)
     4	- **Date:** 2026-11-09
     5	- **Decided by:** owner of this submission, after the independent review (`work/07-review.md`; OD26, OD27)
     6	- **Scope:** pull requests to `main` of the monorepo; the `approval-gate` required check
     7	
     8	## 1. Context
     9	
    10	ADR-0003 made the merge to `main` the approval gate, with an on-call group that co-owns every
    11	deployable path, so that one primary can approve any fix at night. GitHub accepts an approval from
    12	any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve any domain's PR, and the
    13	`incident` label that was meant to limit this can be applied by anyone with Triage (📖 R9.1.9).
    14	ADR-0010 kept one approver for every level. The review also found that a compromised plugin or
    15	local MCP server runs on every laptop and could give an attacker many GitHub logins at once
    16	(threat T23), so a single approval on the files that define the process is one stolen login away.
    17	A path-scoped reviewer rule was not found for GitHub Team (📖 R9.1.15), and the ruleset's approval
    18	count is repository-wide.
    19	
    20	## 2. Options considered
    21	
    22	| Option | Pros | Cons |
    23	|---|---|---|
    24	| A. Keep process rules and the monthly report | No new logic | The label is free to apply; the report misses labelled PRs; one login changes the process |
    25	| B. Raise the ruleset to two approvals for every PR | Built into GitHub | Doubles review for every change, against S4 and the owner's two-person rule |
    26	| C. The approval-gate app, already required, checks the rules per file | Exact rules per path; works on Team | More logic in a custom app that every merge depends on (G19) |
    27	
    28	## 3. Decision
    29	
    30	Option C [design]. The app's decision logic is examples E12 (`examples/approval-gate/gate.py`):
    31	
    32	- an approval counts only if it is on the head commit, by a human who is not the author, the last
    33	  pusher or the person who triggered an app-opened PR (📖 R9.1.10 for the review fields);
    34	- every changed file needs a counted approval from one of its owner teams;
    35	- an on-call group member's approval counts for another team's file only if the PR carries the
    36	  `incident` label, links an incident that is open when the check runs, and the approver is on
    37	  shift (OD27);
    38	- a file owned only by the L3 owner team (a process path) needs two different members of that
    39	  team (OD26);
    40	- approvals within two minutes of the last push, or at night without an incident, are flagged for
    41	  the monthly report, not blocked.
    42	
    43	## 4. Consequences
    44	
    45	- **Positive:** domain review on normal days and the two-person rule on process paths are enforced,
    46	  not trained; the incident lane cannot be opened by a label alone; flagged approvals give a
    47	  detection signal for rubber-stamping and stolen logins.
    48	- **Negative / trade-offs:** process-path PRs need two L3 owner team members; a cross-team PR on a
    49	  normal day needs an owner of each team (OD10's single approval now holds only in incidents);
    50	  a stale schedule or incident record blocks a night approval until the backup or a domain owner
    51	  approves; every merge depends more on the app.
    52	- **Risks & how we watch them:** if the app is down, every merge is blocked, incident PRs included,
    53	  and the JIT fallback applies (layer 7); its hosting, key and triggers stay open (G19); the schedule
    54	  file is an L3 path; the monthly report lists every `incident` PR and every flagged approval.
    55	- **Next steps:** the app becomes a hard prerequisite in phase 1, before the ruleset requires its
    56	  check (rollout).
    57	
    58	## 5. References
    59	
    60	- Framework layer 3 ("L3 approvals", "Who approves at night"), layer 4 ("Pinning what every
    61	  laptop runs"), layer 7 (on-call); threat model T7, T23.
    62	- Related: ADR-0003, ADR-0006, ADR-0010.

| [0007](0007-agent-settings-are-hygiene-not-the-boundary.md) | Claude Code managed settings are hygiene, not the security boundary | 2 |
